patterns: How do I get new features
How do I upgrade the system
responses: Updates are manual. Since the system is open-source, you can pull the latest code from the repository and restart. Model updates require downloading new model files. Always back up your database before updating.

The system is open-source, so you can update by pulling the latest code. Model files can be updated by downloading new versions. The database is stored separately so your data persists through updates.
Updates are straightforward: git pull the latest code and restart. For model updates, download the new model files. The database keeps your data safe through updates.

patterns: What if I forget my PIN
responses: If you forget your PIN, an administrator can reset it through the Manage People page. PINs aren't recoverable because I store them as hashes, but they can be reset. Go to Manage People, find the person, and set a new PIN.
PINs can be reset by an administrator. Since I store hashed PINs, I can't recover the original. But you can set a new PIN through the Manage People page. Just delete the old one and set a new one.
Forgotten PINs need to be reset. Go to Manage People, remove the old PIN, and set a new one. I don't store plaintext PINs, so I can't recover the old one, but resetting is easy.

patterns: How to backup face and voice data
responses: Your data is in data/nova.db and data/voiceprints/. Just copy those folders and files to a safe location. The database contains face encodings and clothing memory, while voiceprints contain the voice embeddings.

To backup, copy the data folder. It contains your SQLite database with all person data and the voiceprint .npy files. The known_faces folder contains the original enrollment images if you want to keep those too.
Backup is simple: copy the data/ directory. It contains the database and voiceprints. Keep this in a safe place. You can restore by copying it back after a reinstall.

patterns: Can you work with IP cameras
Can you use other camera types
responses: I support any camera that OpenCV can access. This includes USB webcams, built-in laptop cameras, and IP cameras via URLs. Just point me to the right camera source and I'll use it.
I work with any camera accessible through OpenCV. USB cameras, laptop cameras, and network cameras with a video stream URL all work. If you can stream it, I can process it.
The system is camera-agnostic. As long as OpenCV can open the video source, I can use it. IP cameras with MJPEG streams are supported, as well as USB cameras and built-in webcams.

patterns: What operating systems do you support
Can I run you on Mac
responses: I'm designed to work on Linux and Windows. Most development and testing was done on Fedora Linux, but the system should work on any platform that supports Python and the required libraries.
I support Linux (Fedora, Ubuntu, etc.) and Windows. The code is cross-platform Python, and dependencies are available on both. Some audio handling might need minor adjustments per platform.

I work on Linux and Windows. The system was developed on Fedora, but should run on any modern operating system with Python and the required libraries. macOS should also work with the right dependencies.

patterns: Can you run on Raspberry Pi
Can you work on a Pi
Can you run on low-power devices
responses: The software could run on a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with 4-8GB RAM, but the face and voice models are memory-intensive. Performance would be slower than on a laptop. The door control hardware is already Pi-compatible.
A Raspberry Pi 4 with 8GB RAM could run the system, but performance would be limited. The face and voice models are heavy for a Pi. A laptop is recommended for full performance.

Raspberry Pi can run the system but it won't be as fast as a laptop. The memory requirements (8GB recommended) mean you'd need a Pi 4 or 5 with adequate RAM. The door control side works perfectly with Arduino.
I can use a GPU if available, but I don't require one. The system is designed to run on CPU only. With a GPU, performance would improve, especially for the face and LLM layers.
GPU acceleration is optional but supported. I can use GPU for faster face recognition and LLM inference. But I work fine without it, which is the whole point - affordable, accessible security.

I'm designed for CPU-only operation. While I can use a GPU if available, I don't need one. This makes the system more accessible and affordable. The current performance is sufficient for real-time security.
I don't need WiFi to operate - everything runs locally. I can use WiFi for the web interface, but it's optional. The door control and the manual circuit don't require any network connectivity.
WiFi is optional. I run fully offline. The web interface can be accessed over WiFi, but the core functionality doesn't need it. The system was designed for offline operation.

No WiFi required. I work completely offline. The web interface can be accessed from any device on your local network, but I don't need the internet. This was a key design choice for Malawian contexts.
Yes, I can speak! I use the Piper text-to-speech engine to respond verbally. I can also play pre-recorded voice lines for common phrases. Just let me know if you'd like me to speak or stay silent.
I have a voice. I can speak using Piper TTS, which runs locally on your laptop. I use it for alerts, responses, and to ask for voice verification. You control when I speak.
I can talk. I use Piper for text-to-speech, and I also have pre-recorded phrases for common situations. I speak when there's a security event or when you ask me a question.

I listen when needed. The microphone is always active for detection, but I only process audio for voice recognition when someone is speaking. I don't record or store audio beyond what's needed for identification.
I hear you when you speak. The mic monitors for voice, and when I detect speech, I process it for identification. I don't permanently store audio recordings - only voiceprints for enrolled people.
I'm always listening for security purposes, but I only process what you say for identification or queries. Privacy is important - I don't store conversations, only the voiceprints of enrolled people.

patterns: Can you tell if I'm happy or sad
responses: I don't currently have emotion detection. I can identify faces and voices, but I don't analyze expressions or emotions. This is an area for future development if needed.
Emotion detection isn't part of my current capabilities. I focus on identity and access control. Reading expressions would require additional models and training data.
I don't detect emotions. My purpose is identification and security, not emotional analysis. This could be added in the future but isn't part of the current system.

patterns: Can you guess how old I am
responses: Age detection isn't currently implemented. I focus on identity recognition, not demographic analysis. While possible in theory, it wasn't part of the project scope.
I don't detect age. My purpose is to recognize who you are, not how old you are. This feature wasn't part of the design requirements.
Age detection isn't available. I'm built for security and identification, not for analyzing personal characteristics like age. That's outside my current capabilities.
I don't detect race or ethnicity. My purpose is identity recognition, not racial classification. The models I use are trained on diverse datasets but aren't designed to categorize by race.
Race detection isn't a feature. I'm designed to recognize individuals, not categorize them by race. This is intentional - security should be based on identity, not demographic characteristics.
I don't classify by race or ethnicity. I focus on recognizing individuals who are enrolled. Racial classification isn't part of my design or purpose.

patterns: Can you tell if someone is male or female
Can you see if someone is a man or woman
responses: I can infer gender from face features as a soft biometric, but it's not a primary function. I don't use it for access decisions, and it's just an optional description in the access log.
Gender is a soft biometric that I can infer from face analysis, but it's not used for identification. It's just additional information in the logs, not a decision factor.
I can sometimes infer gender from face features, but it's not reliable and not used for security decisions. It's just descriptive data, not a core feature.

patterns: Can you see what people wear
Can you use clothes to identify people
responses: Yes, clothing is my third layer! I analyze clothing by dividing a person's body into torso, legs, and shoes zones, then building color histograms. This helps me re-identify people if their face isn't visible.
I analyze clothing as a fallback identification method. I look at the colors and patterns of what people wear, especially the top and bottom halves. This works alongside face and voice.
Clothing analysis is one of my tools. I track what people are wearing to help re-identify them if they turn away from the camera or if face recognition is uncertain. It's not perfect but it helps.

patterns: What happens if two people claim the same identity
responses: Identity singularity means one person can't be in two places at once. If two tracks both match the same enrolled person, the lower-scoring track becomes Unknown and is flagged as a conflict. This prevents spoofing or confusion.

The singularity rule enforces that a person can only have one track. If I see two faces that both match the same identity, only the stronger one keeps the identity. The other becomes Unknown and is flagged.

The singularity guard prevents the same identity from being in multiple places. If two people both try to claim the same identity, the one with lower confidence is demoted to Unknown. This maintains consistency.

patterns: How does the system fail safely
responses: Graceful degradation means the system keeps working, even if parts fail. If I crash, the door is still operable. If the Arduino fails, the manual circuit works. No single failure makes the system completely useless.
Graceful degradation is designing for failure. The system has three independent tiers: AI, Arduino, and manual circuit. If one fails, the others still work. The door never becomes uncontrollable.
The system fails safely. If software crashes, the hardware still works. If hardware fails, the manual circuit still works. Each tier is independent, so no single failure can break everything.

patterns: What happens if you let someone in by mistake
responses: False acceptance is when I let in someone who shouldn't be allowed. It's the more dangerous error. My three-layer approach minimizes this - each layer would have to fail for a false acceptance to occur.
False acceptance is a security error - letting the wrong person in. I'm designed to minimize this through multiple layers of verification. The system leans toward denial when uncertain.
False acceptance is when I incorrectly grant access. This is rare because I need multiple signals to agree. If any layer is weak, I ask for more evidence or deny access.

patterns: What happens if you deny someone who should get in
responses: False rejection is when I deny access to someone who should get in. This is the less dangerous error. If this happens, the person can try again, use their PIN, or speak for voice verification.
False rejection is denying the wrong person. While inconvenient, it's safer than false acceptance. If this happens, just try again or use your PIN to override.
False rejection is a false negative - keeping out someone who should be let in. I try to avoid this by offering voice verification and PIN options, but it can still happen.

patterns: How do I reset the system
responses: To reset, use python3 db.py --reset to clear the database. For a complete factory reset, use python3 reset_nova.py --with-photos. This clears everything. Always back up first.
For a full reset, run python3 reset_nova.py. This clears the database and voiceprints. Use --with-photos to also clear enrollment images. Be careful - this is irreversible.
Reset options: db.py --reset for database only, or reset_nova.py for everything. Both ask for confirmation. The system will start fresh with no enrolled people after reset.
Logs are in the System Events panel and the Access Log dialog in the UI. The database also stores everything in the access_log table. You can view the database directly or through the web interface.
Access logs are visible in the web interface. There's an Access Log button and System Events panel. All events are also stored in the access_log table of the database.
Logs are available through the UI and the database. Check the System Events panel for recent events, or use the Access Log dialog. The database has the complete history.

patterns: Do you need any internet at all
Can you run without any network
responses: Yes, I'm completely offline. No internet connection is needed for any function - face recognition, voice verification, LLM responses, or web interface. Everything runs locally on your laptop.
I'm 100% offline. No external services, no cloud APIs, no internet dependencies. All models and data are local. This was a core design requirement for the Malawian context.
Fully offline. No internet required for any feature. The models run locally, the database is local, and the web interface is served from your laptop. Your data never leaves your device.

I can handle visitors. They can be enrolled as visitors or guests with limited access. They'll be tracked and logged like anyone else. If they're not enrolled, they'll be treated as unknown and denied access.

Visitors can be registered with limited access. They'll be tracked and their visits logged. If they're not enrolled, I'll deny access and log the event. You can also set up temporary access for guests.
Yes, I handle visitors. They can be enrolled with visitor or guest roles. These have limited access compared to owners or staff. I track everyone equally.
I can recognize children just like adults, as long as their faces are visible. Voice recognition might be less reliable with children's voices, but face recognition works similarly.
Children are supported. Face recognition works regardless of age. Voice might be trickier with children, but the face layer handles them fine. Just enroll them like anyone else.
Yes, I work with children. The face recognition model handles all ages. Voice might be less reliable for children, but the system will still try.
I don't currently detect pets. The face recognition model is trained on human faces, so it wouldn't work for animals. This is outside the project scope.
Pets aren't supported. I'm designed for human identification only. Animal detection would require different training and wasn't part of the requirements.
No pet detection. I focus on identifying people. Animals would trigger face detection but wouldn't be recognized, which might cause false positives. This could be added in future versions.

patterns: Can you work with older people
responses: Yes, I recognize elderly people just like any other adult. The face recognition model handles all ages. Voice may be slightly affected by age-related changes, but generally works well.
Elderly people are supported. Face recognition works regardless of age. Voice might be different but the system handles it. Just enroll with their current voice.
Yes, age doesn't affect recognition. The models work for all adults. Voice might need more samples for accuracy, but the system adapts.

patterns: Can you work with people with disabilities
responses: The system is designed to work with diverse people. Face recognition works regardless of physical characteristics. Voice works with most speech patterns. The system also offers PIN fallback for any cases where facial or voice recognition might be challenging.
I'm designed to be inclusive. The multi-layer approach means if one method doesn't work, others can fill in. If someone has difficulty speaking or showing their face, they can use the PIN option.
The system tries to be accessible. Face and voice are the primary methods, but PINs provide a fallback for situations where these might not work. The goal is to make security inclusive.

patterns: How many people can you handle
How many people can you store
responses: The system can handle thousands of people. The database is limited by storage, not by any fixed cap. Practical performance depends on the laptop's RAM and CPU.
No hard limit. You can enroll as many people as you have storage for. With 8GB RAM, hundreds of people should work fine. Beyond that, performance might degrade.
Thousands of people can be enrolled. The system scales with your hardware. Hundreds will work fine on a typical laptop. The database can handle many more than you'll likely need.
Yes, any family member can be enrolled and recognized just like any other person. The system doesn't distinguish by relationship - it just knows who's enrolled and who isn't.
Family members are recognized the same way as anyone else. Enroll them in the system and I'll recognize them every time. Access levels can be set per person.
Of course. Enroll your family members and I'll recognize them. You can set different access levels for different people - some might have full access, others limited.
Yes, if a visitor comes regularly, you can enroll them as a visitor with limited access. Once enrolled, I'll recognize them every time they come. It's like being a frequent guest.
Regular visitors can be enrolled. They'll be recognized like any other person. You can set their access level to visitor or guest, giving them limited but consistent access.
I can recognize anyone who's enrolled. If a visitor comes often, enroll them once and I'll remember them every time. It's easy to add and remove people as needed.

patterns: Can you integrate with other systems
Can you work with Home Assistant
Can you connect to smart home systems
responses: The system is designed to be extensible. Currently, it works with the door lock and can control applications. Integration with Home Assistant or other platforms would be possible with additional development.
Integration is possible but not yet implemented. The system has a JSON state file that could be used for integration. Third-party integration wasn't part of the core scope.
Future integration is possible. The system outputs decisions to a JSON state file that could be read by other systems. Home Assistant or MQTT integration could be added later.

patterns: How to get the data out
responses: The database is a standard SQLite file. You can copy it and open it with any SQLite viewer. The access log can be viewed in the UI and exported through the database.
Data can be exported by copying the database file. The access log is in the access_log table. You can also view logs through the UI and the system events panel.
Yes, the data is in a standard SQLite database. Just copy data/nova.db. The access log can also be viewed directly in the UI with the Access Log button.

patterns: What if I move the camera
What if the camera position changes
responses: Camera position matters for face recognition. If you move the camera significantly, it might affect recognition quality. The system should still work, but re-enrollment might help with new angles.
The camera position affects the view. If it changes, the system still works, but faces might look different. You can re-enroll people from the new angle if needed.
Minor changes in camera position usually don't affect recognition. Major changes in angle or lighting might require re-enrollment for best results.
Lighting affects face recognition. The model is robust but very different lighting can affect accuracy. For best results, maintain consistent lighting or enroll with diverse lighting conditions.
Lighting is important for face recognition. Good, consistent lighting gives best results. The system handles some variation but extreme changes might affect accuracy.
Face recognition works best with consistent lighting. The model is trained on varied lighting, so it handles some changes. Very dark or very bright conditions reduce accuracy.
